newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Russian anti-war mothers share Alternative Nobel Prize.
newsitem.headline: Russian anti-war mothers share Alternative Nobel Prize.

text.p: Russian soldiers' mothers, southern Indian development activists and a Greek homeopathic doctor will share an award known as the Alternative Nobel Prize, the prize donor said on Wednesday.
The Right Livelihood Award, organised to coincide with the Nobel Prizes, aims to reward those who challenge "prevailing orthodoxies in economics, health, peace and human development."
The award, created in 1980 by Swedish-German philatelist Jakob von Uexkull who sold a valuable stamp collection to fund the prize, is now also financed by donations.
A five-member jury decided that three groups would share the $250,000 prize.
The Committee of Soldiers' Mothers of Russia was recognised for its campaigns for "humane conditions in Russia's armed forces and...courageous efforts to end the war in Chechnya."

The group, started in 1989, called for reforms in the Russian armed forces after witnessing beatings, lack of food, and effective slavery imposed on some battalions, the Right Livelihood Award Foundation said in a statement.
"They did what many other mothers of soldiers throughout history have dreamed about doing -- saving their sons from war," Uexkull told a news conference.

The group had also successfully negotiated with the Chechen army about the release of prisoners of war and in their most controversial move, campaigned to encourage mothers to support their sons in refusing military service, the foundation said.
A group of 60,000 Indian teachers, activists and scientists in the state of Kerala was cited for its "crucial contribution to Kerala's successful model of people-centred development".

The group, Kerala Sastra Sahithya Parishat, is involved in projects such as promoting science teaching, organising nutrition programmes, campaigning for environmental awareness and other grass roots activities.
Greek doctor George Vithoulkas would receive the award for "an outstanding contribution to the revival of classical homeopathy."
Vithoulkas, educated at the Indian Institue of Homeopathy, started Greece's International Academy for Classical Homeopathy.

"He has established homeopathy in Greece as a science respected by the medical profession, and also made his country one of the leading centres for homeopathy in the western world," the foundation said.
U.S. environmental economist Herman Daly receives an Honorary Award, which carries no cash prize, for his work which "provides a profound challenge to conventional economic wisdom."

University of Maryland-based Daly was honoured for his approach "that integrates the key elements of ethics, quality of life, environment and community, in contrast to the mainstream obsession with quantitative economic growth and free trade."
The Right Livelihood Awards will be presented at a ceremony in the Swedish Parliament on December 9, one day before the awarding of the Nobel Prizes.
